notes: Demo files are stored in Git LFS (see .gitattributes). Clone with `git lfs install` first, or the .dem files arrive as ~130-byte pointer stubs.

ONE SPECIMEN PER CATEGORY, DELIBERATELY. The corpus was 10 demos and 308 MB; it is now 4 and 14.5 MB. Six of the ten were protocol-24 SourceTV recordings differing only in map and date, and they cost 257 MB to say the same thing six times. GitHub's free Git LFS tier is 1 GiB of bandwidth a month, and every CI job that fetches the corpus spends the whole of it in three runs - so the redundancy was not free, it was the budget.

KEEP ERA SPECIMENS SHORT. The committed corpus is small because its recordings are two to four minutes, not because old clients produce small files. Measured across these entries, size per minute spans 5x: 0.18-0.23 MB/min for SourceTV on a listen server, 0.34-0.92 for POV (which carries dem_usercmd, one input record per tick, where SourceTV carries none), and 0.59 for a 24-player SourceTV match. The same recordings at 30 minutes would make this corpus 90 MB rather than 20. Every protocol-conditional rule fires during signon and the first snapshots, so a short recording exercises the era just as well as a long one - length buys nothing an era specimen needs.

ERA x POINT OF VIEW, which is the shape the committed corpus is kept in. SourceTV and POV are different containers - only POV carries dem_usercmd - so a difference seen in one mode is not an era finding until the other mode agrees. Protocols 11, 14, 16 and 24 have both; protocol 15 has POV only, and a SourceTV recording on the 2009 client would complete it.

Per D5, every entry records how its era was established. Date demos from seasonal asset names in their string tables, never from protocol numbers - protocol 3 / network 24 spans at least 2013 through 2026 and dates nothing. Better still, date the CLIENT: three of the four entries here were recorded on period builds whose `version` command reports an exact date, which is how the era axis was closed at both ends (D30).
Reproduce any field below with `python tools/inspect_demo.py walk|date <file>`.

What was removed is not lost - it is in git history, and the sources are recorded in each entry. Restore a demo if a specific question needs it, rather than keeping six against the possibility. The differential comparison in tools/differential/ ran across four demos and 204,000 properties when it found the flattening-order bug; it now has fewer files to work with, which is a real cost and the reason to re-add one deliberately if that tooling is used again.

The remaining gaps are protocols 12-13, 17, 20 and 23, with no specimen at all: 12-13 inside the five weeks after launch (October to November 2007), 17 between June and November 2011, 20 in November 2011, 23 between build 5126 and March 2013. Protocols 18, 19, 21 and 22 are verified on lcor demos (docs/TIMELINE.md). A protocol-conditional rule stays unexecuted on its far side wherever a gap borders it. Candidate builds are dated from `bin/engine.dll` before downloading (D30). Anything found there is the one category worth ADDING; another modern demo is not.

A SECOND AXIS WITH NO SPECIMENS: server MODS. Every demo here is vanilla, and a mod is not a variation on vanilla - it is a server that changed the rules the replay has to reproduce. Measured 2026-08-27 under D104: a vanilla competitive server already sends 40 convars in net_setconvar, including sv_client_predict, sv_client_max_interp_ratio, sv_mincmdrate and sv_minupdaterate, without touching movement at all. A mod that changes movement sends those too, and this viewer decodes every one of them and consumes none (D106).

The owner's scoping of that, 2026-08-27: 'the only mods we might currently work with are DM and MGE, because those keep most things constant, but jump, surf, and other mods might not run right.' So the prediction is that deathmatch and MGE replay correctly today and jump and surf do not - which is a testable claim with no test, because neither kind is in the corpus. ONE jump demo and ONE surf demo would settle it. Both belong in lcor rather than here: they are protocol-24 recordings and cost LFS bandwidth for a question that is about convars rather than about the container.

Two related notes for whoever adds them. A POV recording DOES carry net_setconvar - measured on ten of benroads' match demos, 32 to 40 values each - so an empty result means the server changed nothing rather than that the point of view dropped it; the era POVs here are empty because they are solo recordings. And surf and jump demos are also the audience for exact tick, angle and input reproduction (docs/memory/surf-and-jump-are-an-audience.md), so one specimen serves two open questions at once.

demos.source: recorded by the owner 2026-08-10 on TF2 build 3258, listen server
demos.whyItMatters:
The oldest specimen in the corpus and the launch build of the game. It also corrected a wrong assumption: the March 2008 build reports protocol 14, and this one was expected to report 14 as well. It reports **11**, so protocols 12 and 13 came and went inside a five-month window between October 2007 and March 2008.

It decodes end to end with no rule changes at all, which is the substantive result. Every protocol-conditional branch this parser has is keyed on 14 or above, so protocol 11 exercises all of them on their old side simultaneously - the absent string table compression flag, the six-bit schema bit-count field, the five-bit message type, the old SendPropType numbering, the four-byte map CRC, the 13-bit prefetch index and fixed lengths. Nothing below 14 needed a new rule.

demos.whyItMatters: The oldest SourceTV recording in the corpus, and the control that turned a suspected POV quirk into an era fact. It carries NO dem_stringtables command, exactly as the protocol-14 POV demo does and unlike every protocol-15 or 24 file - so the absence is a property of the era, not of the recording mode. One demo could not have established that. It also carries no dem_consolecmd and no dem_usercmd at all, which is the structural difference between SourceTV and POV: nobody is pressing keys.
demos.notes: Recorded on a listen server with `tv_enable 1` before the map load, then `tv_record`. No dedicated server was needed and no period srcds binary had to be found: the client packs ship tf/bin/server.dll and the engine already exports tv_enable, tv_record and tv_maxclients. That is the route to a SourceTV specimen for any era whose client runs.

demos.notes: Carries NO dem_stringtables command, where the 2009 and 2013 entries each carry exactly one. At protocol 14 the tables arrive only as svc_CreateStringTable in the signon stream. Not documented in proto_version.h and not predicted - the same discovery shape as RISKS B17 and B18. It also disproved a fingerprint: the string table COUNT is 16 here, in the 2009 demo and in modern demos alike, so it dates nothing. Max classes does move: 216 here, 232 in 2009, 275 modern.

demos.source: recorded by the owner 2026-08-10 on TF2 build 4604, listen server
demos.whyItMatters:
The first specimen from inside the 16-23 gap, and 16 is the most valuable single value in it. svc_ServerInfo's replay flag is read as `protocol > 15`, so **16 is the first protocol that carries it** - every other entry tests that rule from a distance, 14 and 15 from below and 24 from well above, and a boundary is only really tested at the value where it changes. It decoded end to end, which it could not have done had the flag been read wrongly: everything after it would have desynchronised.

It also holds a combination no other entry can - new SendPropType numbering and a six-bit message type TOGETHER WITH a 13-bit svc_Prefetch index and fixed temp-entity lengths. That is exactly the interpolation the 15-to-24 jump forced the parser to assume.

demos.notes: This file found a real bug on first read. Its recording player's name contains a non-ASCII character, and the dump printed it two different ways in one output - `mia??ker` from the header, which read ASCII, and correctly from the userinfo table, which read UTF-8. Nothing failed; both were plausible names. Every string decoder is UTF-8 as of that fix, and the disagreement between two decoders was the only signal.

corpusGaps.preTwentyTwenty: EMPTY, and not for lack of trying. Checked 2026-08-07: RGL launched 2019 so its oldest demos are the same era as these. ETF2L's listing goes back to Sept 2014 but the files have rotted - every demo id below ~12010 returns HTTP 404, and the live floor is id 12025, dated 2020-07-23. ESEA's SourceTV demos shipped with expiry dates and were never permanently downloadable, so there is nothing to recover; community Mega collections catalogued on teamfortress.tv in 2013 are long dead. sizzlingstats, which did keep demos, is gone.
corpusGaps.consequence: The parser has no historical coverage and no test that would reveal its absence. See D5 - the schema-driven design has to be right by construction, because it cannot be verified.

verifiedButNotStored.why: These parse end to end and are recorded for auditability, but are not committed. Git LFS on the free tier allows 1 GB of storage and 1 GB of bandwidth per month; the stored corpus is already ~316 MB and every fresh clone spends that against the bandwidth allowance. Test value is per-map and per-quirk rather than per-file, and these five duplicate maps already covered.
